7. Comparison and human-work target

I gave comparators the same service interfaces and allowed them to adopt the useful setting, isolation and recovery primitives.

Conditional comparison at 5,000 episodes/year	Cost/episode	Human work/year
Candidate	$42.37	73.24 h
Assisted exchange using identical hardware	$46.76	487.70 h
Automated adopter of the same complete primitive	Parity	Parity
Adopter with 25% lower installed capital	$40.45	Same introduced labor boundary
Favorable competent shoring/clamp cases	$16.87–30.82	Depends on 5–15 active minutes

The favorable cases use introduced capital and labor assumptions. They are neither supplier quotations nor evidence that an equally capable unattended product is commercially available.

They do show that the candidate cannot establish an economic advantage merely because a matched commercial quotation is unavailable. Under those assumptions, assisted work would need approximately 25–27 active minutes per exchange before reaching candidate cost parity.

The human ledger is:

Human work	Hours/year
Preparation, mastering, stock and inspections	47.27
Physical renewal labor	20.97
In-window retained-support callouts	5.00
Total	73.24

The tenfold target allows 48.77 h/year. Another 24.47 h/year of real operations would have to disappear or become demonstrably unattended. Deleting the callout line would not suffice.

Sensitivity
Case	Conditional cost/episode
Electricity $40/MWh	$42.36
Electricity $80/MWh	$42.37
Electricity $160/MWh	$42.38
Half annual throughput	$53.22
Half assumed component life	$57.25
Double failure frequency	$55.26
Exclusive operator allocation	$69.64
2,000 scheduled h/year, 90% availability	$43.62
2,000 scheduled h/year, 60% availability	$49.64

At the modeled cycle time, 5,000 episodes require approximately 2,189 scheduled hours at 90% availability. A 2,000-hour year supports about 4,568 episodes; at 60% availability, about 3,046.

The new local primitive therefore has no established whole-service advantage over a competent adopter.
